title: Google faces new UK lawsuit over online display ads
content:
The case argues that Google favoured its own display advertising services while excluding its rivals (Idrees MOHAMMED)

Google faces a fresh UK lawsuit accusing it of abusing its dominance in online display advertising, the claimants announced Thursday, in the latest antitrust action against the US tech giant.

The claim filed on behalf of British advertisers is seeking up to £3 billion ($4 billion) in compensation, according to an estimate from KP Law, the firm leading the action.

The case argues that Google favoured its own display advertising services, such as banner ads shown on websites, while excluding its rivals.

KP Law said Google's practices left "advertisers paying more for less effective display advertising".

A Google spokesperson called the allegations "meritless".

"Advertisers have many choices, and they choose our ad tech tools because they're simple, effective and affordable," the spokesperson said.

The case has been brought as a collective action, meaning all potentially affected clients are automatically included unless they choose to opt out.

It covers all UK advertisers who have paid for Google's advertising services since October 1, 2015.

The claim was yet to be formally served, according to Google.

The company's advertising practices have been the subject of multiple investigations and legal proceedings in the UK, the European Union and the United States.

A separate lawsuit filed in UK courts last year also accused Google of overcharging for online advertising.

Other cases on similar grounds are ongoing, including a £13.6 billion claim brought on behalf of online content publishers, which was cleared in 2024 to proceed to trial.

Google is also facing efforts by the US government to break up its digital advertising business to curtail its dominance.

Last year, the EU hit Google with a massive 2.95-billion-euro antitrust fine for favouring its own advertising services.

Google has said it will appeal the fine.

title: Moonshot AI Raises $2 Billion As Valuation Tops $20 Billion
content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Moonshot AI has raised about $2 billion in its latest funding round, marking another sharp signal that investor appetite for China's AI challengers continues to build. The round was led by the venture arm of food delivery leader Meituan (MPNGY), lifting Moonshot's valuation to more than $20 billion, according to a statement from financial adviser HF Capital, which advised some of the backers. The company's annual recurring revenue topped $200 million in April, supported by subscriptions to its Kimi chatbot and AI model services. That combination could make Moonshot one of the more closely watched private AI companies in China, especially as investors continue looking for local players that may be able to rival Silicon Valley leaders.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 4 Warning Sign with HLFFF. Is GOOG fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

The pace of Moonshot's valuation increase is what makes this funding round particularly notable. The Beijing startup raised $500 million at a $4.3 billion valuation toward the end of last year, followed by another $700 million at a $10 billion valuation earlier this year, before seeking an additional $1 billion in an expanded round, Bloomberg News reported. With the latest round now valuing the company above $20 billion, Moonshot has more than quadrupled its valuation in just a few months. A Moonshot spokesperson did not respond to messaged requests for comment, while a representative with Meituan's Long-Z Investments confirmed its participation.

The broader AI funding backdrop in China could be just as important for investors. DeepSeek is in the process of raising outside capital for the first time, drawing interest from state investors at a valuation of as much as $50 billion. Public-market peers MiniMax and Zhipu AI have also surged to valuations of more than $30 billion since their Hong Kong debuts in January. Moonshot was founded by Yang Zhilin, a former Tsinghua University professor who previously worked at Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) and Alphabet's Google (NASDAQ:GOOG), and the company sells tiered subscription plans for its chatbot while also offering its underlying technology to enterprise clients.

title: Microsoft Reconsiders Energy Goal Amid AI Boom
content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) is reportedly reconsidering one of its biggest climate goals as the AI driven data center boom pushes energy demand to new levels.

According to reports, the company is discussing whether to delay or potentially abandon its 2030 target of matching 100% of its hourly electricity usage with renewable energy purchases. The conversations are still ongoing and no final decision has been made, but the debate itself highlights how quickly AI infrastructure demands are reshaping energy priorities across Big Tech.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 1 Warning Sign with MSFT. Is MSFT fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

The challenge comes down to scale. Microsoft has been adding nearly 1 gigawatt of data center capacity every 3 months as it races to support AI and cloud growth. That rapid expansion is increasing both electricity usage and emissions, despite major renewable energy investments. Since the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022, Microsoft's emissions have reportedly risen 23%, with the company itself pointing to AI and cloud expansion as major contributors.

At the same time, the industry is increasingly leaning toward natural gas to meet near term power needs. Companies like Amazon (AMZN), Meta (META) and Google (GOOG) are also facing growing pressure as AI workloads surge. Microsoft says it remains committed to its long term sustainability ambitions, but also acknowledged that adjustments may be needed as markets and technology evolve.
